title: Asynchronous I/O
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of asynchronous i/o in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to async http requests.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers asynchronous i/o within asynchronous programming and concurrency. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use asynchronous i/o to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is resource lifecycle, cancellation, concurrency limits and observable I/O behavior.

content_blocks.title: Asynchronous I/O: concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step flow for Asynchronous I/O: Async HTTP requests, Async database drivers, Managing connections, Concurrent I/O operations
content_blocks.caption: Visual-first overview before the worked example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Asynchronous I/O matters because it is part of asynchronous programming and concurrency. In practice, focus on resource lifecycle, cancellation, concurrency limits and observable I/O behavior. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Async HTTP requests
items.text: For async http requests, identify which operation waits on I/O, which resources remain open, and what happens on timeout or disconnect. Async syntax does not make CPU-bound work faster or durable background jobs reliable by itself.

items.title: Async database drivers
items.text: Apply async database drivers against a disposable database and synthetic data first. Make transaction ownership and cleanup explicit, parameterize values, and verify constraints and behavior after failures before considering a deployment.

items.title: Managing connections
items.text: Use managing connections as a design decision rather than a keyword to memorize. State the input and expected result, identify the boundary conditions, and connect the concept to the surrounding FastAPI request lifecycle.

items.title: Concurrent I/O operations
items.text: For concurrent i/o operations, identify which operation waits on I/O, which resources remain open, and what happens on timeout or disconnect. Async syntax does not make CPU-bound work faster or durable background jobs reliable by itself.

items.title: Cancellation and timeouts
items.text: For cancellation and timeouts, identify which operation waits on I/O, which resources remain open, and what happens on timeout or disconnect. Async syntax does not make CPU-bound work faster or durable background jobs reliable by itself.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Asynchronous I/O
content_blocks.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///./lab.db")
with engine.begin() as connection:
    result = connection.execute(text("SELECT 1 AS ok"))
    print(result.scalar_one())
content_blocks.run_instructions: This tiny SQLAlchemy connection smoke test uses local SQLite. Use parameterized statements for values; place real credentials in environment configuration.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.
content_blocks.limitations: This code is inspectable lesson material, not executed by CodeLeaf. Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. Security examples are sketches, not complete production authentication or authorization systems.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “Async HTTP requests”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

task: Create a small reviewable artifact for “Asynchronous I/O”: explain its goal, cover the listed subtopics, show an example with expected result, then include one edge case and how you would verify it.
hints: Start with “Async HTTP requests” and state the required inputs, output and assumptions.
Change one thing at a time; check the official reference and capture the actual response/error instead of guessing.
Include a negative/edge-case check and document which behavior remains untested.
expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Asynchronous I/O, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.

summary: Asynchronous I/O belongs to the broader goal of resource lifecycle, cancellation, concurrency limits and observable I/O behavior.
Use the source subtopics as the completeness checklist and verify expected results rather than relying on intuition.
Examples in this course are illustrative until technically reviewed and executed on a supported local environment.
